entities.summary:
Imbert du Puy, a prominent French cardinal in the Avignon Papacy, served as a crucial ecclesiastical and political figure in Western Europe during the first half of the 14th century. Born into a powerful ecclesiastical lineage as the nephew of Pope John XXII (Jacques Duèze), his career was inextricably linked to the zenith of the Avignon Papacy's administrative and financial centralization. Elevated to cardinal-priest of Santi XII Apostoli in December 1327, du Puy's influence extended across the Curia, where he advised his uncle and later popes on matters ranging from church doctrine to diplomatic relations with secular powers, solidifying the institutional power of the papacy from its new French base.

Throughout his cardinalate, Imbert du Puy was deeply involved in the complex political and theological landscape of the early 14th century. He participated in two significant papal conclaves: that of 1334, which elected Benedict XII, and the conclave of 1342, which saw Clement VI ascend to the papal throne. His administrative acumen was vital in managing the vast network of benefices and financial mechanisms that characterized the Avignon system. He held numerous prebends and provostships across France, including the provostship of Saint-Jean-de-Lyon and the archdeaconry of York, demonstrating the reach of papal appointments and the accumulation of wealth by high-ranking ecclesiastics.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Imbert du Puy's career as a cardinal exemplifies the consolidation of papal power and administrative structure during the Avignon Papacy, influencing the selection of two popes and managing significant ecclesiastical wealth. His death during the Black Death also highlights the devastating impact of the pandemic on the Church's leadership.
